claim: Optogenetic theta frequency stimulation (oTFS) induced LTP at Schaffer collateral synapses in rat hippocampal slice cultures.
source: Optical theta frequency stimulation induced LTP at Schaffer collateral synapses
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that oTFS induced LTP, including measurements of EPSCaTs and EPSCs before and after stimulation.

claim: CA3 neurons expressing ChR2(E123T/T159C) together with synaptophysin-tdimer2 were stimulated with short pulses of blue light (2 ms long, 40 ms interval, λ = 470 nm).
source: CA3 neurons expressing the light-sensitive channel ChR2(E123T/T159C) (Berndt et al., 2011) together with the presynaptic vesicle marker synaptophysin-tdimer2 were stimulated with short pulses of blue light (2 ms long, 40 ms interval, λ = 470 nm).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methods used, citing the source of the ChR2 variant.

claim: Light stimulation evoked EPSCs with a magnitude of 1330 ± 220 pA.
source: Light stimulation evoked EPSCs with a magnitude of 1330 ± 220 pA, consistent with our previous study (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments, with reference to consistency with prior work.

claim: TFS-induced LTP requires transient (30 s) stimulation of enough CA3 cells to drive postsynaptic CA1 cells to fire complex spike bursts (CSBs).
source: TFS-induced LTP requires transient (30 s) stimulation of enough CA3 cells to drive postsynaptic CA1 cells to fire complex spike bursts (CSBs, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Thomas et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by both the experimental observations in the manuscript and citation to prior work by Thomas et al., 1998.

claim: EPSCaTs were strongly potentiated 30 min after oTFS.
source: EPSCaTs were strongly potentiated 30 min after oTFS, generating calcium transients that frequently spread into the dendrite (Figure 1B, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The amplitude of EPSCs in the reporter neuron increased after oTFS, indicating successful induction of LTP.
source: Likewise, the amplitude of EPSCs in the reporter neuron increased after oTFS, indicating successful induction of LTP (Figure 1B, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the electrophysiological recordings shown in the figures.

claim: Both CSBs and LTP induction were blocked in the presence of the NMDA receptor antagonist APV.
source: Both CSBs and LTP induction were blocked in the presence of the NMDA receptor antagonist APV (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological manipulation experiments shown in the figures.

claim: oTFS induced plasticity via NMDAR activation as previously demonstrated.
source: Thus, oTFS induced plasticity via NMDAR activation as previously demonstrated (Thomas et al., 1998).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the APV blocking experiments and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: When no large dendritic calcium transients were triggered during oTFS, spine calcium signals were not consistently potentiated 30 min after oTFS.
source: When no large dendritic calcium transients were triggered during oTFS, spine calcium signals were not consistently potentiated 30 min after oTFS (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data comparing conditions with and without dendritic calcium spikes.

claim: EPSCs showed considerably lower trial-to-trial variability (no failures) compared to EPSCaTs.
source: EPSCs, integrating the activity of many synapses, showed considerably lower trial-to-trial variability (no failures) compared to EPSCaTs.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two types of measurements in the experiments.

claim: EPSCaT amplitude and EPSCaT potency were significantly increased 30 min after oTFS in experiments where complex spike bursts (CSBs) were induced during oTFS.
source: EPSCaT amplitude (p=0.0008, n = 20 slice cultures) and EPSCaT potency (successes only, p=0.0025) but not EPSCaT probability (PCa, p>0.05) were increased 30 min after oTFS in experiments where complex spike bursts (CSBs) were induced during oTFS.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data with specific p-values and sample sizes provided.

claim: LTP had no significant effect on the probability of EPSCaT occurrence (PCa).
source: LTP had no significant effect on the probability of EPSCaT occurrence (PCa, Figure 2C), suggesting that the potentiation was mainly due to postsynaptic changes.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The potentiation was mainly due to postsynaptic changes.
source: LTP had no significant effect on the probability of EPSCaT occurrence (PCa, Figure 2C), suggesting that the potentiation was mainly due to postsynaptic changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in release probability (PCa).

claim: In experiments where no CSBs were elicited during oTFS, PCa was significantly reduced.
source: Interestingly, while EPSCaT potency was not affected in experiments where no CSBs were elicited during oTFS, PCa was significantly reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the experimental data.

claim: In experiments where the synaptic drive was not strong enough to trigger postsynaptic spikes, presynaptic activity in the theta frequency range appeared to elicit a weak form of presynaptic depression.
source: Thus, in experiments where the synaptic drive was not strong enough to trigger postsynaptic spikes, presynaptic activity in the theta frequency range appeared to elicit a weak form of presynaptic depression.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in PCa when CSBs were not elicited.

claim: The head volume of spines that experienced CSBs increased by 21 ± 6% during the 30 min after oTFS.
source: The head volume of spines that experienced CSBs was unchanged immediately after oTFS, but increased by 21 ± 6% during the next 30 min.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claim: The nearest neighboring spines showed a small but significant increase in volume (15 ± 3%) after oTFS.
source: The nearest neighboring spines also showed a small but significant increase in volume (15 ± 3%), whereas no consistent change was detected at more distant spines (2 ± 3%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claim: No consistent change in volume was detected at more distant spines (2 ± 3%) after oTFS.
source: The nearest neighboring spines also showed a small but significant increase in volume (15 ± 3%), whereas no consistent change was detected at more distant spines (2 ± 3%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claim: When no oTFS was applied, the volume of responding spines (5 ± 4%) and neighbors (−4 ± 3%) remained stable.
source: When no oTFS was applied, the volume of responding spines (5 ± 4%) and neighbors (−4 ± 3%) remained stable (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a control measurement from the imaging data.

claim: In oTFS experiments that failed to elicit CSBs or when NMDA receptors were blocked during oTFS, stimulated spines did not exhibit significant volume changes.
source: In oTFS experiments that failed to elicit CSBs or when NMDA receptors were blocked during oTFS, stimulated spines did not exhibit significant volume changes (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting similar requirements for the successful induction of functional and structural plasticity.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Spine head volume and EPSCaT potency were significantly increased 30 min after oTFS.
source: Consistent with our first data set, spine head volume and EPSCaT potency were significantly increased 30 min after oTFS (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a replication of the earlier findings in a new dataset.

claim: Twenty-four hours after LTP induction, both spine head volume and EPSCaT potency had returned to baseline.
source: Twenty-four hours after LTP induction, however, both measures had returned to baseline.
evidence: This is an observation from the longitudinal imaging and functional measurements.

claim: No significant change in EPSCaT probability was detected either 30 min or 24 hr after oTFS.
source: We detected no significant change in EPSCaT probability either 30 min or 24 hr after oTFS (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Beyond the acute effects on the day of potentiation, no permanent changes in synaptic strength were observed after oTFS-induced LTP.
source: Thus, beyond the acute effects on the day of potentiation, we did not observe permanent changes in synaptic strength after oTFS-induced LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 24-hour follow-up data.

claim: Under control conditions without external stimulation, 27% of all spines disappeared between days 1 and 7.
source: Under control conditions without external stimulation, 27% of all spines disappeared between days 1 and 7.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: The 27% spine turnover rate is in agreement with previous measurements in hippocampal slice cultures and mouse hippocampus in vivo.
source: This turnover rate is in agreement with previous measurements in hippocampal slice cultures (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013) and mouse hippocampus in vivo (Attardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with published literature.

claim: During the 7 days following LTP induction, only one of 11 potentiated spines disappeared.
source: In a dataset of 14 spines, 11 spines experienced CSBs and were potentiated. During the following 7 days, only one of these 11 potentiated spines disappeared (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: Nearest-neighbor spines disappeared less often between days 1 and 7 compared to controls after LTP.
source: Compared to controls, nearest-neighbor spines disappeared less often between days 1 and 7 whereas more distant spines (>5 µm) were eliminated more often (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: More distant spines (>5 µm) were eliminated more often between days 1 and 7 compared to controls after LTP.
source: Compared to controls, nearest-neighbor spines disappeared less often between days 1 and 7 whereas more distant spines (>5 µm) were eliminated more often (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: Biochemical signaling molecules activated inside stimulated spines during oTFS diffuse into neighboring, non-stimulated spines, affecting acutely their size and on longer time scales, their survival.
source: These findings are consistent with the concept of biochemical signaling molecules activated inside stimulated spines during oTFS and diffusing into neighboring, non-stimulated spines (Nishiyama and Yasuda, 2015), affecting acutely their size and on longer timer scales, their survival.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on established concepts from the literature.

claim: In oTFS experiments where no CSBs were elicited in CA1 neurons, stimulated spines as well as their neighbors had reduced survival rates.
source: In these experiments, stimulated spines as well as their neighbors had reduced survival rates (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: The destabilizing effect of oTFS without CSBs was contingent on 5 Hz presynaptic activation.
source: This destabilizing effect was contingent on 5 Hz presynaptic activation, as spines that were not stimulated at all or only stimulated by test pulses (responsive spines) had higher survival rates (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a comparison of different experimental conditions showing the specificity of the effect.

claim: Optogenetic low frequency stimulation (oLFS, 900 APs at 1 Hz) induced long-term depression (LTD) at Schaffer collateral synapses.
source: As we established previously (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013), optogenetic low frequency stimulation (oLFS, 900 APs at 1 Hz) induced long-term depression (LTD) at Schaffer collateral synapses, frequently abolishing EPSCaTs in the stimulated spine altogether (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a replication of previous findings with reference to prior work.

claim: 45% of spines that received oLFS disappeared between days 1 and 7.
source: In agreement with our previous results, 45% of spines that received oLFS disappeared between days 1 and 7.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: LTD on day 0 was considered successful when the average spine Ca2+ response dropped to less than 90% of the baseline response 30 min after oLFS, which was the case in 70% (28/40) of the experiments.
source: LTD on day 0 was considered successful when the average spine Ca2+ response dropped to less than 90% of the baseline response 30 min after oLFS, which was the case in 70% (28/40) of the experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a definition of success criteria and the quantitative outcome of the experiments.

claim: LTP induction was considered successful when the average spine Ca2+ response increased to more than 110% of the day one baseline response after oTFS, which was the case in 64% (18/28) of all experiments on day 1.
source: LTP induction was considered successful when the average spine Ca2+ response increased to more than 110% of the day one baseline response after oTFS, which was the case in 64% (18/28) of all experiments on day 1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a definition of success criteria and the quantitative outcome of the experiments.

claim: When LTP was induced after LTD, only 12% of spines disappeared between days 1 and 7, indicating stabilization of doomed synapses.
source: When LTP was induced after LTD, only 12% of spines disappeared between days 1 and 7, indicating stabilization of doomed synapses.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the longitudinal imaging data with an interpretation.

claim: Of the spines that received oTFS after LTD but did not get potentiated, 43% disappeared between days 1 and 7, similar to the 45% disappearance rate seen after oLFS only.
source: Of the spines that received oTFS after LTD but did not get potentiated, 43% disappeared between days 1 and 7, similar to the 45% disappearance rate seen after oLFS only.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: Successful LTP induction was necessary to rescue synapses from elimination after LTD.
source: These results confirmed that successful LTP induction was necessary to rescue synapses from elimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the survival rates of spines with and without successful LTP after LTD.

claim: Without LTP, the oTFS stimulation protocol by itself had no measurable effect on the survival of previously depressed synapses.
source: Without LTP, the oTFS stimulation protocol by itself had no measurable effect on the survival of previously depressed synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the survival rates of spines that received oTFS but did not show LTP versus those that only received LTD.

claim: LTP on day 0 was induced in 72% (18/25) of spines after oTFS.
source: LTP on day 0 was induced in 72% (18/25) of spines after oTFS (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), similar to the set of oTFS experiments 1 day after oLFS (64%, p=0.85) and the first set of oTFS experiments (Figure 2B, 62%, 26/42, p=0.41).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation with statistical comparison to other datasets.

claim: When oLFS was applied 24 hr after LTP, LTD was induced in only 33% (6/18) of previously potentiated synapses.
source: When oLFS was applied 24 hr later, we observed that LTD was induced in only 33% (6/18) of previously potentiated synapses on the next day (Figure 5B), a much lower success rate than the 70% when oLFS was applied with no prior plasticity.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation comparing LTD induction rates with and without prior LTP.

claim: The median number of APs in reporter neurons during the 900 pulses of the oLFS protocol was 1.5 in naive cultures (n = 32) and 5.0 one day after LTP (n = 13, p=0.4, Mann-Whitney).
source: The median number of APs in reporter neurons during the 900 pulses of the oLFS protocol was 1.5 in naive cultures (n = 32) and 5.0 one day after LTP (n = 13, p=0.4, Mann-Whitney), corresponding to a postsynaptic spike probability below 1% in both cases.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical analysis.

claim: Strong postsynaptic spiking during the oLFS protocol is not a likely explanation for the difficulty to depress previously potentiated synapses.
source: Thus, strong postsynaptic spiking during the oLFS protocol is not a likely explanation for the difficulty to depress previously potentiated synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of action potential counts during oLFS.

claim: The initial EPSCaT amplitude (before oLFS) was not a predictor of successful LTD induction.
source: However, the initial EPSCaT amplitude (before oLFS) was not a predictor of successful LTD induction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the relationship between initial amplitude and LTD success.

claim: There is a synapse-specific memory of past potentiation events that cannot be detected as increased spine volume, increased release probability or increased EPSCaT potency.
source: These results point to a synapse-specific memory of past potentiation events that cannot be detected as increased spine volume, increased release probability or increased EPSCaT potency (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that previously potentiated synapses resist depression despite having returned to baseline in measurable parameters.

claim: In the few experiments where LTD was successfully induced 24 hr after LTP, 50% of spines disappeared by day 7.
source: In the few experiments where LTD was successfully induced 24 hr after LTP, 50% of spines disappeared by day 7 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: In the more typical case where oLFS failed to induce LTD after LTP, only 8% of spines disappeared by day 7.
source: In the more typical case where oLFS failed to induce LTD, only 8% of spines disappeared by day 7.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: The strength of the synapse on day 0 or on day one did not predict its survival.
source: However, the strength of the synapse on day 0 or on day one did not predict its survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E), leaving successful induction of depression as the only risk factor we could identify.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the relationship between synaptic strength and survival.

claim: The stabilizing effect of LTP on spines can be overwritten by subsequent LTD.
source: In summary, the stabilizing effect of LTP on spines can be overwritten by subsequent LTD (Figure 5C), but this sequence of plasticity events is not very likely to happen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequential plasticity experiments.

claim: LTP and spine-specific stabilization can be induced at 5 Hz if a sufficient number of inputs are activated synchronously.
source: Here we show that LTP and spine-specific stabilization can be induced at 5 Hz, the typical carrier frequency of rodent hippocampus, if a sufficient number of inputs are activated synchronously (Moody et al., 1998; Thomas et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings with reference to prior work on synchronous activation.

claim: Theta-frequency stimulation (TFS) is the physiological equivalent of spike-timing-dependent potentiation (STDP) protocols.
source: We consider theta-frequency stimulation (TFS) the physiological equivalent of spike-timing-dependent potentiation (STDP) protocols, replacing the artificial current injection into the postsynaptic neuron by highly synchronized excitatory synaptic input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental approach in the context of known plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Synchronized synaptic input can trigger dendritic calcium spikes, local regenerative events caused by the opening of voltage-dependent channels (NMDARs and VDCCs).
source: Synchronized synaptic input can trigger dendritic calcium spikes, local regenerative events caused by the opening of voltage-dependent channels (NMDARs and VDCCs).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of dendritic physiology.

claim: Dendritic calcium spikes can be electrophysiologically identified as complex spike bursts, consisting of several fast sodium spikes on top of a broader depolarization mediated by dendritic calcium currents.
source: These events can be electrophysiogically identified as complex spike bursts, consisting of several fast sodium spikes on top of a broader depolarization mediated by dendritic calcium currents (Magee and Johnston, 1997; Golding et al., 2002; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Grienberger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: The occurrence of dendritic calcium spikes during the induction protocol was highly predictive of successful LTP induction at individual synapses.
source: In our experiments, the occurrence of dendritic calcium spikes during the induction protocol was highly predictive of successful LTP induction at individual synapses (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Theta-frequency-modulated synaptic input to CA1 pyramidal cells triggers dendritic calcium spikes which are required for synaptic potentiation and place cell formation in head-fixed mice running on a treadmill.
source: Recent studies in head-fixed mice running on a treadmill suggest that theta-frequency-modulated synaptic input to CA1 pyramidal cells triggers dendritic calcium spikes which are required for synaptic potentiation and place cell formation (Bittner et al., 2015; Sheffield et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited recent studies.

claim: Dendritic calcium spikes during complex spike bursts, evoked by synchronized input from entorhinal cortex and CA3 pyramidal cells, are part of the physiological mechanism for the selective potentiation of active Schaffer collateral synapses during behavior.
source: Thus, dendritic calcium spikes during complex spike bursts, evoked by synchronized input from entorhinal cortex and CA3 pyramidal cells, are part of the physiological mechanism for the selective potentiation of active Schaffer collateral synapses during behavior (Hasselmo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of in vivo physiology, with citation.

claim: Newly inserted AMPA receptors lead to stronger depolarization of the spine head during the EPSP, more efficient unblocking of NMDA receptors and EPSCaT potentiation.
source: Newly inserted AMPA receptors lead to stronger depolarization of the spine head during the EPSP, more efficient unblocking of NMDA receptors and EPSCaT potentiation.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism underlying EPSCaT potentiation based on established knowledge.

claim: EPSCaT amplitudes are not linearly related to somatic EPSCs.
source: It is important to note, however, that EPSCaT amplitudes are not linearly related to somatic EPSCs.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the measurement technique based on known biophysics.

claim: The ratio between AMPA and NMDA receptors is not constant between spines.
source: The ratio between AMPA and NMDA receptors is not constant between spines, and peak calcium concentrations depend on spine head volume and spine neck resistance (Grunditz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from cited work.

claim: High EPSCaT amplitudes can lead to SK channel activation and dampening of the EPSP.
source: High EPSCaT amplitudes can even lead to SK channel activation and dampening of the EPSP (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from cited work.

claim: Postsynaptic failures (successful glutamate release without postsynaptic calcium influx) are thought to be rare at Schaffer collateral synapses.
source: Counting the number of EPSCaTs in a set of stimulated trials can be used as a proxy for presynaptic release probability, as postsynaptic failures (successful glutamate release without postsynaptic calcium influx) are thought to be rare at Schaffer collateral synapses (Nimchinsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from cited work.

claim: In LTD, the reduction in average EPSCaT amplitude was mainly due to decreased release probability.
source: In contrast to LTD, where the reduction in average EPSCaT amplitude was mainly due to decreased release probability (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013), oTFS-induced LTP strongly enhanced EPSCaT potency, but did not seem to affect release probability.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings from cited work.

claim: Postsynaptic mechanisms such as AMPA receptor insertion account for oTFS-induced LTP.
source: This confirms that postsynaptic mechanisms such as AMPA receptor insertion account for this form of potentiation (Shi et al., 1999; Lu et al., 2001; Matsuzaki et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of established mechanisms from cited work.

claim: LTD induction did not affect spine volume.
source: While LTD induction did not affect spine volume (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013), LTP triggered significant growth of the postsynaptic compartment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings from cited work.

claim: Twenty-four hours after induction of LTP, synapses were back to their baseline state with respect to the amplitude and probability of spine calcium transients as well as the volume of the spine head.
source: Twenty-four hours after induction of LTP, synapses were back to their baseline state with respect to the amplitude and probability of spine calcium transients as well as the volume of the spine head.
evidence: This is a summary of the 24-hour follow-up data.

claim: A long-lasting, synapse-specific memory of the potentiation event was maintained 24 hours after LTP, since once-potentiated spines were more likely to persist during the following week compared to other spines on the same dendritic branch, or non-stimulated controls.
source: Yet, a long-lasting, synapse-specific memory of the potentiation event was maintained, since these once-potentiated spines were more likely to persist during the following week compared to other spines on the same dendritic branch, or non-stimulated controls.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the longitudinal survival data.

claim: The effects of LTD may outlast the actual depression: CA1 spines did not show any lasting reduction in volume, but their life expectancy was significantly reduced after LTD.
source: Similarly, the effects of LTD may outlast the actual depression: CA1 spines did not show any lasting reduction in volume, but their life expectancy was significantly reduced after LTD (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings from cited work.

claim: A similar sequence of transient LTD followed by delayed spine elimination was found at the parallel fiber synapse on Purkinje cells in the cerebellum.
source: A similar sequence of transient LTD followed by delayed spine elimination was found at the parallel fiber synapse on Purkinje cells in the cerebellum (Aziz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from cited work in a different brain region.

claim: Information could be robustly stored in the topology of the network rather than in the analog strength of individual synapses.
source: These findings support the theoretical concept that information could be robustly stored in the topology of the network rather than in the analog strength of individual synapses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical concepts.

claim: Synaptic tenacity is known to be affected by trans-synaptic proteins such as Neuroligin-1 and SynCAM-1.
source: Synaptic tenacity is known to be affected by trans-synaptic proteins such as Neuroligin-1 and SynCAM-1 (Zeidan and Ziv, 2012; Körber and Stein, 2016), PSD-95 (De Roo et al., 2008; Cane et al., 2014), ubiquitin protein ligase E3A (Kim et al., 2016), ensheathment of the synapse by astrocyte processes (Bernardinelli et al., 2014) and many other local factors.
evidence: This is a summary of established knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: It may be a combination of local physical changes and distributed network effects, such as the recurrent reactivation of a specific circuit, which makes once potentiated synapses robust against depression and pruning.
source: It may be a combination of local physical changes and distributed network effects, such as the recurrent reactivation of a specific circuit (Wei and Koulakov, 2014; Novitskaya et al., 2016), which makes once potentiated synapses robust against depression (Figure 5B) and pruning (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanisms underlying the observed phenomena, with citations.

claim: The link between LTP and long-term structural stability on the single-synapse level could explain why learning-induced spines in motor cortex are more stable than their pre-existing neighbors and persist for months after training.
source: The link between LTP and long-term structural stability we show on the single-synapse level could explain why learning-induced spines in motor cortex are more stable than their pre-existing neighbors and persist for months after training (Xu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of in vivo learning studies, with citations.

claim: LTP-induced tenacity might be a general principle to connect different time scales of cortical circuit plasticity.
source: LTP-induced tenacity might be a general principle to connect different time scales of cortical circuit plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization of the findings.

claim: Failure to evoke postsynaptic CSBs upon oTFS led to presynaptic depression, which was followed by increased spine elimination.
source: Failure to evoke postsynaptic CSBs upon oTFS led to presynaptic depression in our experiments, which was followed by increased spine elimination (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Presynaptic depression following oTFS without CSBs is mediated by autocrine glutamate signaling at the presynaptic terminal and may not involve postsynaptic signaling.
source: This effect has been shown to be mediated by autocrine glutamate signaling at the presynaptic terminal and may not involve postsynaptic signaling (Padamsey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism based on cited work.

claim: If the postsynaptic neuron is driven to spike, retrograde signaling via NO (nitric oxide) leads to an increase in release probability.
source: If, on the other hand, the postsynaptic neuron is driven to spike, retrograde signaling via NO (nitric oxide) leads to an increase in release probability, which explains why we did not see presynaptic depression in synapses that experienced CSBs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: The classical Hebbian rule of rewarding only synapses that causally contribute to postsynaptic AP firing also seems to apply to long-term stability.
source: Thus, the classical Hebbian rule of rewarding only synapses that causally contribute to postsynaptic AP firing also seems to apply to long-term stability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of Hebbian learning theory.

claim: Changes in spine properties are not perfectly confined to the directly driven synapse: oTFS not only affected strength, volume and long-term stability of the stimulated spines, but also increased volume and stability of its immediate neighbors.
source: However, our results suggest that changes are not perfectly confined to the directly driven synapse: Optogenetic TFS not only affected strength, volume and long-term stability of the stimulated spines, but also increased volume and stability of its immediate neighbors (Figure 2D, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The spread of plasticity effects to neighboring spines is consistent with short-range diffusion of 'potentiating factors' such as activated RhoA and Cdc42 out of the directly stimulated spine.
source: This is consistent with short-range diffusion of 'potentiating factors' such as activated RhoA and Cdc42 out of the directly stimulated spine (Murakoshi et al., 2011; Yasuda, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of known molecular mechanisms, with citations.

claim: More distant spines on the same dendrite (5–10 µm) showed no increase in volume and a decrease in lifetime after LTP.
source: In contrast, more distant spines on the same dendrite (5–10 µm) showed no increase in volume and a decrease in lifetime (Figure 2D, Figure 3E), confirming an earlier 3 day study (De Roo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with reference to a prior study.

claim: The 7 day follow-up points to a center-surround function that stabilizes the immediate neighbors (<5 µm) of potentiated synapses, although they were most likely not active during the induction protocol.
source: Nevertheless, our 7 day follow-up points to a center-surround function that stabilizes the immediate neighbors (<5 µm) of potentiated synapses, although they were most likely not active during the induction protocol (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial pattern of spine survival data.

claim: LTD-induced destabilization has a larger (>10 µm) lateral spread than LTP-induced stabilization.
source: As we have previously shown, LTD-induced destabilization has an even larger (>10 µm) lateral spread (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013).
evidence: This is a reference to previous findings from cited work.

claim: The local environment is as important for the long-term survival of a synaptic connection as its own activity history.
source: Apparently, the local environment is as important for the long-term survival of a synaptic connection as its own activity history.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of lateral spread of plasticity effects.

claim: It might be impossible to prune a synapse next to a strongly potentiated spine.
source: This could put a limit to the uniformity of synaptic inputs in dendritic sections, as it might be impossible to prune a synapse next to a strongly potentiated spine.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the implications of the findings.

claim: Synaptic pruning is not a random process, but determined by the last plasticity-inducing activity pattern.
source: By inducing two rounds of plasticity, we demonstrated that synaptic pruning is not a random process, but determined by the last plasticity-inducing activity pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequential plasticity experiments.

claim: In the organotypic culture system, the latency between LTD induction and spine loss was several days.
source: In the organotypic culture system, the latency between LTD induction and spine loss was several days.
evidence: This is an observation from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: The latency between LTD induction and spine loss could be considerably shorter in vivo, given the highly rhythmic activity of the hippocampal circuit and in consequence, intense synaptic competition.
source: This period could be considerably shorter in vivo, given the highly rhythmic activity of the hippocampal circuit and in consequence, intense synaptic competition.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the in vitro findings to the in vivo situation.

claim: The experimental approach complements in vivo studies of structural plasticity, which provide information about spine turnover, but not about the activity patterns in pre- and postsynaptic neurons.
source: Our approach allows imposing any kind of spike pattern to a select group of synapses over several days. It complements in vivo studies of structural plasticity, which provide information about spine turnover, but not about the activity patterns in pre- and postsynaptic neurons (Attardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the experimental approach, with citation.

claim: Networks with self-organized connectivity might generate activity patterns that are different from the randomly connected networks underlying current large-scale simulations.
source: Networks with self-organized connectivity might generate activity patterns that are different from the randomly connected networks underlying current large-scale simulations (Markram et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications for network modeling, with citation.

claim: Long-term analysis of the structure-function relationship of individual synapses may help understanding how the brain stores and retrieves memories.
source: Together with realistic simulations of synaptic network dynamics and long-term investigations of synapse remodeling in vivo, long-term analysis of the structure-function relationship of individual synapses may help understanding how the brain stores and retrieves memories.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of this type of research.

claim: Graded changes in synaptic strength, driven by specific activity patterns, are a candidate mechanism for information storage in the brain.
source: Graded changes in synaptic strength, driven by specific activity patterns, are a candidate mechanism for information storage in the brain (Chaudhuri and Fiete, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of a theoretical concept from the literature.

claim: When entire pathways are potentiated by high frequency stimulation, the increase in synaptic coupling can be recorded for several days.
source: When entire pathways are potentiated by high frequency stimulation, the increase in synaptic coupling can indeed be recorded for several days (Bliss and Lomo, 1973).
evidence: This is a reference to classic findings in the field.

claim: Increases in the size of synapses, the number of postsynaptic transmitter receptors and release of transmitter have been shown to underlie increases in synaptic strength.
source: Increases in the size of synapses, the number of postsynaptic transmitter receptors and release of transmitter, have been shown to underlie increases in synaptic strength.
evidence: This is a summary of established knowledge about the mechanisms of synaptic strengthening.

claim: A prevailing theory is that graded changes in synaptic strength persist as a memory trace of former activity.
source: A prevailing theory is that graded changes in synaptic strength persist as a memory trace of former activity.
evidence: This is a statement of a prevailing theoretical view in the field.

claim: Dramatic fluctuations in spine volume over time scales of hours to days cast doubt on whether information can be stored for long periods in the analog strength of synapses.
source: At the level of individual synapses, however, dramatic fluctuations in spine volume over time scales of hours to days cast doubt on whether information can be stored for long periods in the analog strength of synapses (Holtmaat and Caroni, 2016; Berry and Nedivi, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of a challenge to the prevailing theory, with citations.

claim: An alternative hypothesis is that over longer time periods, information is stored not in the strength but in the number of connections, which, at the level of individual synapses, would manifest as a change in synaptic lifetime.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that over longer time periods, information is stored not in the strength but in the number of connections, which, at the level of individual synapses, would manifest as a change in synaptic lifetime.
evidence: This is a statement of an alternative theoretical hypothesis.

claim: Long term depression (LTD) decreases synaptic lifetime.
source: Supporting evidence comes from the findings that long term depression (LTD) decreases synaptic lifetime (Nägerl et al., 2004; Bastrikova et al., 2008; Wiegert and Oertner, 2013) and that spine structure becomes stabilized and growth persists up to 3 days after induction of long term potentiation (LTP) (De Roo et al., 2008; Hill and Zito, 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Spine structure becomes stabilized and growth persists up to 3 days after induction of long term potentiation (LTP).
source: Supporting evidence comes from the findings that long term depression (LTD) decreases synaptic lifetime (Nägerl et al., 2004; Bastrikova et al., 2008; Wiegert and Oertner, 2013) and that spine structure becomes stabilized and growth persists up to 3 days after induction of long term potentiation (LTP) (De Roo et al., 2008; Hill and Zito, 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: LTP can be reversed by low-frequency stimulation (depotentiation), but such depotentiation may only occur 1–2 hr after LTP induction.
source: For example, LTP can be reversed by low-frequency stimulation (LFS), but such depotentiation may only occur 1–2 hr after LTP induction (Fujii et al., 1991; O'Dell and Kandel, 1994; Abraham and Huggett, 1997; Zhou et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: How a once potentiated synapse responds to LFS one day later is difficult to predict.
source: How a once potentiated synapse responds to LFS one day later is therefore difficult to predict.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that motivated the study.

claim: Schaffer collateral synapses were potentiated by 5 Hz stimulation if complex spike bursts were induced in the postsynaptic CA1 neuron.
source: Using organotypic hippocampal slice cultures and optical stimulation of channelrhodopsin-expressing CA3 pyramidal neurons, we found that Schaffer collateral synapses were potentiated by 5 Hz stimulation if complex spike bursts were induced in the postsynaptic CA1 neuron (Thomas et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding, with citation to prior work on the requirement for CSBs.

claim: During successful synaptic transmission, Ca2+ ions enter the spine through voltage-gated calcium channels and NMDA receptors which both have a steep dependence on membrane depolarization.
source: During successful synaptic transmission, Ca2+ ions enter the spine through voltage-gated calcium cannels and NMDA receptors which both have a steep dependence on membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about spine calcium dynamics.

claim: EPSCaTs depend on AMPA receptor activity and can be used to detect changes in synaptic strength.
source: Thus, EPSCaTs depend on AMPA receptor activity (Holbro et al., 2010) and can be used to detect changes in synaptic strength (Emptage et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the measurement technique, with citations.

claim: Compared to glutamate uncaging experiments, which only report changes in postsynaptic strength (potency), optogenetic interrogation is also sensitive to presynaptic changes (release probability), providing a more complete picture of synaptic transmission.
source: Compared to glutamate uncaging experiments, which only report changes in postsynaptic strength (potency), optogenetic interrogation is also sensitive to presynaptic changes (release probability), providing a more complete picture of synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the experimental approach.

claim: LTD and LTP differentially affected synaptic lifetime.
source: As suggested by previous studies, LTD and LTP differentially affected synaptic lifetime.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, with reference to prior studies.

claim: Sequentially inducing LTD and LTP did not return spines to their basal state, but resulted in reduced elimination rates similar to synapses which only underwent LTP.
source: However, sequentially inducing LTD and LTP did not return spines to their basal state, but resulted in reduced elimination rates similar to synapses which only underwent LTP.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the sequential plasticity experiments.

claim: Once LTP was induced, it became almost impossible to induce subsequent LTD.
source: Once LTP was induced, it became almost impossible to induce subsequent LTD.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the sequential plasticity experiments.

claim: In the few experiments where LTD could be induced 24 hr after LTP, synaptic lifetime was similar to that of spines that only underwent LTD.
source: In the few experiments were LTD could be induced 24 hr after LTP, synaptic lifetime was similar to that of spines that only underwent LTD.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the sequential plasticity experiments.

claim: Multiple weight adjustments are not summed in a linear fashion, but the most recent plasticity event determines the lifetime of a Schaffer collateral synapse.
source: Thus, multiple weight adjustments are not summed in a linear fashion, but the most recent plasticity event determines the lifetime of a Schaffer collateral synapse.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the sequential plasticity experiments.

claim: Hippocampal slice cultures from male Wistar rats were prepared at postnatal day 4–5.
source: Hippocampal slice cultures from male Wistar rats were prepared at postnatal day 4–5 as described (Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: At DIV 3, rAAV2/7 encoding ChR2(ET/TC)−2A-synaptophysin-tdimer2 was pressure-injected into CA3.
source: At DIV 3, we pressure-injected rAAV2/7 encoding ChR2(ET/TC)−2A-synaptophysin-tdimer2 into CA3.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: At DIV 18, single-cell electroporation was used to transfect CA1 pyramidal neurons with GCaMP6s and mCerulean (ratio 1:1).
source: At DIV 18, single-cell electroporation was used to transfect CA1 pyramidal neurons in rAAV-infected slices with GCaMP6s and mCerulean (ratio 1:1) as described (Wiegert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Experiments were performed between DIV 21 and 25.
source: Experiments were performed between DIV 21 and 25.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Whole-cell recordings from CA1 pyramidal cells were made at 25°C with a Multiclamp 700B amplifier.
source: Whole-cell recordings from CA1 pyramidal cells were made at 25°C with a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: LTD experiments were conducted in ACSF containing (in mM) 135 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 4 CaCl2, 4 MgCl2, 10 Na-HEPES, 12.5 D-glucose, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 0.03 D-Serine (pH 7.4, sterile filtered).
source: LTD experiments were conducted in ACSF containing (in mM) 135 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 4 CaCl2, 4 MgCl2, 10 Na-HEPES, 12.5 D-glucose, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 0.03 D-Serine (pH 7.4, sterile filtered).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: During LTP induction, ACSF with lower divalent ion concentration (2 CaCl2, 1 MgCl2) was used to increase excitability.
source: During LTP induction, ACSF with lower divalent ion concentration (2 CaCl2, 1 MgCl2) was used to increase excitability.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Recordings with a drift of >20% in access resistance were discarded.
source: Access resistance was monitored continuously and recordings with a drift of >20% were discarded.
evidence: This is a description of the quality control criteria for the experiments.
